title: Reference — ScrumIA
meta_description: ScrumIA reference: the twelve modules and their skills, the roles, the config file, and how to write your own module.
page_intro: Modules, skills, configuration, and how to write your own.
core_p: Fills no slot and does nothing on its own. It describes the composition and makes it legible to agents. The only non-optional module.
core_row1: Installs or checks the composition, generates the CLAUDE.md section
core_row2: Inspects, changes or diagnoses the composition
rules_p: Sits beside scrumia-core: the rules-hierarchy format itself — index, guides, decisions — that lets a module's knowledge skill, or a project's own conventions, load only the guide a task routes to instead of one growing file. Fills no slot. Assumes nothing beyond scrumia-core. Costs one more layer to author correctly — a section is overhead below three distinct concerns.
rules_row1: The format reference: anatomy, navigation, precedence between sections — read first
rules_row2: Scaffolds a project-local section: interview, harvest from code and lint configs, write, register in CLAUDE.md
rules_row3: Evolves a rule: challenges its decision, refines or supersedes it, updates the guide, logs the change
specs_p: Per-feature specs, TDD-oriented. A contextual file catalogue rather than one document. Assumes specs live in the repo next to the code. Costs more judgement when writing than a fixed template.
specs_row2: Creates, updates or audits a feature
specs_row3: Finds a rule, walks dependencies, loads minimal context
ghp_p: Issues, sub-issues, GitHub Projects columns, branches and PRs. A PreToolUse hook blocks stateful files in the repo. Assumes an authenticated gh. Costs a hard GitHub dependency and nothing offline.
ghp_row2: Moves a ticket from Backlog to Ready for dev
ghp_row3: Runs a ticket: worktree, spec, code, tests, review, PR
ghp_row4: Routes a PR review and synthesises
teams_manager_p: Board, splitting, routing, cadence. Doesn't own business rules, architecture, or the merge.
teams_business_p: Rules, vocabulary, compliance. Doesn't own architecture, stack, or planning.
teams_tech_p: Architecture, contracts, debt, quality. Doesn't own business rules or priorities.
teams_p: Each boundary is a line of refusal — without it, the three collapse into one generalist and the split stops paying for itself. Three isn't a magic number: roles are enabled, disabled and added by config. Turning one off is a documented trade-off, not a downgrade.
teams_row1: Active roles, their models, escalation rules
teams_row2: Builds a sprint and consumes it in dynamic workflows
disc_row1: Challenges an idea until it can be split
disc_row2: Splits into features, creates issues, ships specs on a branch
rust_p: Invalid states made unrepresentable, Result at the boundaries, typed errors per layer. Refuses unwrap() in production, clones that appease the borrow checker, single-implementer traits.
rust_row1: The reference, loaded before writing Rust in a covered app
rust_row2: Measures an existing app against the rules, finding by finding
solidjs_p: Fine-grained reactivity without React reflexes, behaviour-first component tests, structure by feature. Refuses destructured props, effects used as derivations, components that fetch.
reactjs_p: Server Components by default, Actions for mutations, derived state during render, behaviour-first component tests. Refuses useEffect for derived state, imperative DOM, effects where event handlers belong, unnecessary "use client".
solidjs_row1: The reference, loaded before writing SolidJS in a covered app
solidjs_row2: Measures an existing app against the rules, finding by finding
reactjs_row1: The reference, loaded before writing React 19 in a covered app
reactjs_row2: Measures an existing app against the rules, finding by finding
tdd_p: Refines one point of the implementation contract: how we test. The cycle operationalized for an agent, the mock boundary, AC-to-test mapping.
tdd_row1: The reference: cycle, mock boundary, where TDD stops
tdd_row2: The real state of an app's test safety net
tdd_row3: Puts a zone under test before touching it
solid_p: Refines one point of the implementation contract: which design principles. The five principles, each with its application limit — over-application is audited on equal footing with violations.
solid_row1: The reference: the five, with their limits, in OO and functional alike
solid_row2: Violations and over-applications, on equal footing
solid_row3: Resolves one finding, in safe steps
tanstack_p: Refines one point of the implementation contract: how the app talks to the server and caches what it gets back — query keys, invalidation, optimistic updates, the boundary against client-only state. Ported from real monorepo use: 9 guides, 13 decisions. Assumes a stack TanStack Query ships for (React, Solid, Vue, Svelte). Costs a caching model to learn — the audit and refactor skills that would measure and close the gap aren't built yet.
tanstack_row1: The reference: query keys, cache invalidation, optimistic updates, the server/client boundary
compound_p: The compound component pattern, framework-agnostic. A parent exposes its parts through a single API, children reach the parent through context (or the framework's equivalent — provide/inject, signals, a service), and sub-components travel with the parent rather than being scattered across module paths. Documented side by side for React, Vue, Solid and Angular, in each framework's idiom.
compound_row1: Takes stock of an existing component: does it read like a compound? Are the parts co-located? Is the public API one symbol?
rhf_p: Declarative form management for React apps using React Hook Form. Refuses a form without a resolver, useState + onChange where register() already covers it, and state read through the DOM. Scoped to scrumia-impl-reactjs; a SolidJS app pays no cost.
rhf_row1: Measures an existing React app against the three refusals — resolver, registration, state channel
config_intro: .scrumia/config.yaml describes the project and its tooling — never its state.
config_note: Two conventions that matter: the mapping names what is present, so a capability you go without carries no key at all — and where the difference between "not chosen yet" and "deliberately without" matters, it is said as a comment standing in the key's place. And every module documents the keys it reads under settings: an implicit setting is one you can't change.
impl_title: Implementation modules and the modules that refine them
impl_intro: The most personal choice. An app lists the modules it draws on — its implementation module, and any number of others that sharpen one point of what that module says. Two competent developers can hold opposite views here and neither is wrong, which is exactly why these are replaceable modules rather than kernel rules.
impl_contract_p: A skill the agent loads before writing code in that app, covering four things:
impl_li1: How you test — which level for which change, what gets stubbed and what doesn't, how an AC-n becomes a test
impl_li2: Which design principles — named and situated. "We apply SOLID" guides nobody; a principle without a boundary becomes a reflex, and reflexes produce needless abstraction
impl_li3: How code is laid out — precise enough that an agent places a new file without hesitating
impl_li4: What is refused — the most useful part, and the most often skipped. An agent that knows what's rejected self-corrects
impl_compose_p: A module can refine one named point of that contract — scrumia-tdd refines "how you test", scrumia-solid-principles refines "which design principles" — and ship the reference, the audit and the refactor skills that go with it. The implementation module situates each for its stack. One precedence rule: specific beats generic — the implementation module over the module refining it, the project override over both.
impl_override_p: Every module documents what it reads under its own params:, plus an optional project override file (.scrumia/modules/<module>.md) whose content it honours over its own rules. A module offering neither gets forked at the first disagreement — and that fork never sees an update.
design_p: Identity, tokens and components live in the repo; a Claude Design project is the review surface, not the source of truth. One rule underneath: a value the tokens don't carry is a finding, never an inlined exception. Ships the designer standing role — the only module that does so from outside the team slot, because a role with no design system to guard would judge on taste.
design_row1: Creates the tree, writes the identity, registers the role
design_row2: The reference: what lives where, the four questions before writing a component
design_row3: Pushes and pulls components through DesignSync, one at a time
design_row4: Audits an existing interface: drift and mutedness, two columns
html_css_p: The HTML, CSS and accessibility capability for a covered app. Three refusal rules and one audit skill: a semantic element when both express the same intent, an interactive widget that uses the element whose contract matches the action, and a test that queries what an assistive technology would meet. Scoped to React and SolidJS by default; a project running neither pays no cost.
html_css_row1: Audits a covered app's HTML/CSS against the three refusal rules
impl_note_p: The two contracts touch without overlapping: the implementation module owns how a component is written, scrumia-design owns what it looks like. A SolidJS component and a server-rendered template consume the same tokens.
rules_hier_p: Each knowledge skill becomes a routing index instead of one fat file: 00-index.md loaded first and always, guides/NN-topic.md loaded only on demand, decisions/D-NN-slug.md opened only when a rule is challenged. A section.json declares the globs a section governs. In a monorepo, an app's path in apps[] anchors which sections apply where — the same specific beats generic precedence, one level down. See scrumia-rules above and ADR-0011.
write_li1: Fill a slot — an existing one, or a new one you define and document
write_li3: Provide your CLAUDE.md line — the sentence that tells an agent what it needs without reading you
write_prohibition: And one prohibition: never assume another module is present. If a capability is missing, say so and propose the next step rather than failing.
write_newslot: A new slot is warranted when a real project would fill it differently. Otherwise it's one more skill in an existing module.
zod_p: Runtime validation at the trust boundary. The type is derived from the schema rather than hand-written beside it, parsing happens where untrusted data enters rather than on every internal call, and a schema whose failure a user reads carries a field-targeted message. Cited against Zod pinned to v4.
zod_row1: Audits an existing codebase against the three refusals: schemas duplicated as hand-written types, user-facing boundaries with no field-targeted errors, and parses on values the compiler already proved.
gradle_p: Gradle the build tool, stated in Gradle's terms. Eight refusals or norms: Kotlin DSL over Groovy, version catalog as the one place versions live, the shape of a convention plugin (precompiled script plugin in a build-logic composite), lazy task configuration, the build and configuration caches, composite builds for local siblings, pluginManagement, and documentation tasks wired into the lifecycle. The Kotlin Multiplatform-specific application of these rules belongs to scrumia-kotlin-multiplatform-mobile, cited here only as where the shape is applied.
gradle_row1: Audits an existing Gradle project against the eight rules — find each .gradle Groovy file, each literal version, each eager tasks.create, each missing cache flag, each plugin version declared in the wrong place
material3_p: Material 3 the UI system, stated in Material 3's terms. Eight refusals or norms: Compose as the default toolkit and Views as an explicit choice with a stated justification; tokens from MaterialTheme.colorScheme, Typography, Shapes, elevation, and the state-layer system — never from hex literals; components from androidx.compose.material3.* — never built from primitives; dynamic color as the default on Android 12+; touch targets of 48dp × 48dp; contrast ratios of 4.5:1 for body text and 3:1 for large text; and contentDescription on every icon-only control.
material3_row1: Audits an existing Android or Kotlin Multiplatform Mobile surface against the eight rules — find each View-based widget without a stated justification, each hardcoded color or typography step, each reinvented Button or Card or AppBar, each static brand palette on Android 12+, each interactive control below 48dp, each contrast ratio below WCAG AA, each IconButton without a TalkBack label
kmm_p: The Kotlin Multiplatform Mobile composition preset. Six refusals: expect/actual stays in commonMain for the contract and in the platform source set for the implementation; source-set layout keeps platform code in its own source set; platform tests and shared dependencies live where they compile for every target; a Cocoapods pod is declared once across the KMP module and the iOS project; the target list is the one in the Gradle DSL, not the one an IDE invents; Gradle wiring goes through the Kotlin Multiplatform plugin's source-set DSL.
kmm_row1: Six rule families — expect/actual across source sets, source-set layout, platform tests and dependencies, Cocoapods and Swift interop, target declaration, KMP-shaped Gradle wiring — each its own file, all citing the Kotlin documentation
ktor_p: HTTP server and client rules for a Ktor codebase. Nine refusals or norms: the application's surface is one routing {} block split into nested route extension functions; ContentNegotiation is installed once per application and per client; one HttpClient per remote dependency, built once and closed once; authentication is install(Authentication) { name -> ... } with named providers; route tests run on testApplication {}; ports, hosts, secrets and URLs come from environment.config; a streaming route states whether it is WebSocket or SSE; request logging is install(CallLogging) with a filter; and an HTTP non-2xx is converted into a domain error in one named place.
ktor_row1: Audits an existing Ktor project against the nine rule families — find each route registered outside the routing tree, each hand-rolled parse on call.receiveText(), each per-call HttpClient, each Authorization header read inside a handler, each test that opens a real port, each literal host or secret in code, each WebSocket body that never reads a frame, each println in a handler, each Result.failure whose body is r.status
